behavior_items: The provided reproducer text does not contain a concrete C++ program; it only names the feature under test: C++26 expansion statements from P1306R5. That means the exercised behavior is best understood as front-end support for the new statement form rather than a specific runtime algorithm.

P1306R5 introduces a statement-level pack expansion facility, so the compiler work involved is primarily parsing new syntax in statement context, building the corresponding AST representation, and performing semantic analysis for repeated execution of a statement body over pack elements or other expandable entities.

A conforming implementation must distinguish expansion statements from existing pack expansion forms used in expressions, declarators, base-specifiers, or lambda captures. The reproducer therefore likely probes whether GCC accepts the new grammar in the correct syntactic positions under a C++26 language mode and rejects it in earlier modes.

Semantic analysis for expansion statements must model how names introduced inside the repeated statement are instantiated for each expansion step, how pack element substitution occurs, and how scope/lifetime rules interact with each repetition. Bugs in this area often appear as incorrect name lookup, substitution failures, or invalid diagnostics about packs not being expanded.

The compiler must also determine whether the expansion target is a valid pack-like entity, whether all referenced packs have compatible lengths when multiple packs participate, and whether the repeated statement body is well-formed after substitution for every element. A reproducer for this feature commonly exercises these validity checks.

Because expansion statements are a core language feature, the reproducer likely stresses parser recovery and feature gating as much as semantic correctness: GCC should recognize the syntax only when the selected standard enables C++26 support for P1306R5, and it should produce a precise diagnostic rather than misparsing the construct as unrelated syntax.

If the bug is a failure rather than an acceptance issue, the likely faulty subsystem is the C++ front end: tokenization of the new syntax, parser integration with statement grammar, template/pack substitution machinery, or AST lowering for repeated statements. No backend or runtime behavior can be inferred from the supplied text alone.

test_failure_analysis.analysis: The common pattern is that every available clue points to a missing or incorrect C++ front-end implementation of a new core-language feature, not to ordinary code generation. The reproducer, bug report, and observed failure all name only P1306R5 expansion statements, so the failure most likely occurs when GCC tries to recognize, gate, parse, represent, or semantically validate a statement-level pack expansion in C++26 mode. Expansion statements are unusual because they add pack expansion in statement context rather than in already-supported expression or declarator contexts. That creates several likely fault lines: the parser may not admit the new grammar in statement position; feature gating may reject valid C++26 syntax or accept it in the wrong language modes; the AST may lack a dedicated node or may incorrectly reuse expression-pack machinery; semantic analysis may mishandle per-expansion scope, name lookup, substitution, or pack-length checks; and diagnostics may be emitted from older pack-expansion code paths that do not understand statement forms. Since no concrete program or runtime behavior is given, the most probable bug class is incomplete or miswired front-end support for P1306R5 in parsing and semantic processing.

gcc/cp/decl.cc.summary: We're initializing a local variable which has a cleanup GUARD. If there are any temporaries used in the initializer INIT of this variable, we need to wrap their cleanups with TRY_CATCH_EXPR (, GUARD) so that the variable will be cleaned up properly if one of them throws. Unfortunately, there's no way to express this properly in terms of nesting, as the regions for the temporaries overlap the region for the variable itself; if there are two temporaries, the variable needs to be the first thing destroyed if either of the temporary destructors throws. However, we only want to run the variable's cleanup if it actually got constructed. So we need to guard the temporary cleanups with the variable's cleanup if they are run on the normal path, but not if they are run on the exceptional path. We implement this by telling honor_protect_cleanup_actions to strip the variable cleanup from the exceptional path. Another approach could be to make the variable cleanup region enclose initialization, but depend on a flag to indicate that the variable is initialized; that's effectively what we do for arrays. But the current approach works fine for non-arrays, and has no code overhead in the usual case

We store accesses in one of the two lists: PBEFORE_SP, and PNO_SP. If this expression or its only operand forces a sequence point, then everything up to the sequence point is stored in PBEFORE_SP. Everything else gets stored in PNO_SP. Once we return, we will have emitted warnings if any subexpression before such a sequence point could be undefined. On a higher level, however, the sequence point may not be relevant, and we'll merge the two lists. Example: (b++, a) + b; The call that processes the COMPOUND_EXPR will store the increment of B in PBEFORE_SP, and the use of A in PNO_SP. The higher-level call that processes the PLUS_EXPR will need to merge the two lists so that eventually, all accesses end up on the same list (and we'll warn about the unordered subexpressions b++ and b. A note on merging. If we modify the former example so that our expression becomes (b++, b) + a care must be taken not simply to add all three expressions into the final PNO_SP list. The function merge_tlist takes care of that by merging the before-SP list of the COMPOUND_EXPR into its after-SP list

The bug report points to missing or incorrect front-end parsing and diagnostics for a new statement form, and those responsibilities most likely live somewhere inside this large parser region.

Expansion statements introduce new syntax in statement context, where GCC must correctly distinguish the construct from declarations and other existing grammar forms. If the parser classifies the leading tokens incorrectly here, valid C++26 expansion statements could be rejected or misparsed through older declaration-oriented paths.

Expansion statements introduce a new statement-form in statement context, and this routine is the central hook for inserting C++ statements into the statement tree.
